checks.claim: Killed (inactivated), live attenuated and subunit vaccines as described
checks.note: Subunit vaccines 'only expose the patient to the key antigens of a pathogen'.

checks.claim: Key: all give an antigen, a shape the body's own cells learn to recognise (artificial active immunity)
Wrong choice: antibodies made in another body = artificial passive immunity ('transfer of antibodies produced by a donor', human or animal; used for tetanus, botulism, diphtheria toxins)
Wrong choices: donor white cells; a medicine that kills the germ - not what a vaccine is
Context: matching B cells multiply, plasma cells make antibodies, memory cells remain
Primary response slow (days to weeks; peak 5-10 days); secondary faster (2-5 days) and larger (10-100-fold titres)
checks.note: Grokipedia also gives 100-1000-fold elsewhere; the question keys no fold figure.

checks.claim: Key: memory B cells formed after the first dose, which 'swiftly differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells'
Wrong choices: leftover antibody, stored antigen, immune system stronger with age - not the cause
checks.note: OpenStax: the secondary response is 'initiated by memory B cells'.

checks.claim: Context: inactivated vaccines 'usually require higher doses and multiple boosters'
Montagu had her son Edward engrafted at the Constantinople embassy, March 1718 (surgeon Charles Maitland)
Onesimus, enslaved West African man (likely Akan), told Cotton Mather of inoculation through a cut
Boylston lost about 2 in 100 (6 of 247-248, 2.4 %); natural smallpox killed about 1 in 7 (844 of 5,759, 14.7 %)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 5,889 cases, 14.3 %. Both round to about 1 in 7.

checks.claim: Jenner 75 years later (1721 + 75 = 1796)
Key: cowpox did away with giving real smallpox that could kill or spread
checks.note: Variolation gave real smallpox and could spread it; cowpox vaccination was 'far safer' and 'far more rarely transmitted to their contacts'. OpenStax: variolation cases could be 'serious and sometimes fatal'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Jenner still used cuts ('two small cuts'); still took matter from a person's sore (Sarah Nelmes's hand); lifelong protection proved wrong (revaccination needed)
checks.note: Revaccination: Wikipedia, Smallpox vaccine ('rashly claimed that the protective effect was lifelong').

checks.claim: Benjamin Jesty, Dorset farmer, 1774, Yetminster epidemic: cowpox matter scratched into the arms of his wife Elizabeth and two eldest sons
checks.note: Riedel (PMC1200696) gives 'a small lancet', Wikipedia 'a darning needle'; the stem only says 'scratched'.

checks.claim: Jenner, country doctor at Berkeley; 14 May 1796, matter from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes's hand into eight-year-old James Phipps, his gardener's son
Donald Hopkins quote: 'Jenner's unique contribution was not that he inoculated a few persons with cowpox, but that he then proved [by subsequent challenges] that they were immune to smallpox.'
checks.note: Matches Wikipedia word for word (Hopkins, The Greatest Killer, 2002, p. 80). The bracketed words are an editor's insertion, as the brackets show.

checks.claim: Key: Jenner tested with smallpox matter and published; Jesty did not publicise
checks.note: Holds as stated. Note: Jesty's sons were later exposed and two 'were later challenged with smallpox by variolation and were unaffected' (Pead 2014, PMC3883152; Robert again in 1805), so the challenge alone was not unique; the publication half makes the key true.

checks.claim: Context: 1 July 1796 smallpox challenge, no disease; 23 cases in the self-funded 1798 Inquiry after the Royal Society rejected the 1797 paper
checks.note: Wikipedia: findings on 23 cases.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: explained the mechanism (no one could); a whole village (no); persuaded Parliament (compulsion came only with the Vaccination Act 1853, 30 years after his 1823 death)
Last natural case Somalia 1977 (Ali Maow Maalin, Merca, 26 Oct 1977)
33rd World Health Assembly declared eradication on 8 May 1980 (certified December 1979); the only human disease eradicated
Key: no animal reservoir, only people
checks.note: WHO factsheet: 'There is no animal reservoir. Insects play no role in transmission.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: not everyone vaccinated (surveillance-containment); stocks still kept at CDC and VECTOR; no insect vector
Distinctive rash made cases easy to find
checks.note: 'distinctive rash enabling reliable identification'

checks.claim: William Foege, American (CDC) doctor, eastern Nigeria, outbreak in December 1966, too little vaccine
checks.note: Emory dates it 4 December 1966; some CDC accounts say early 1967 (Ogoja). 'Late in 1966' fits the main accounts.

checks.claim: Officials believed '80 to 100 percent of the population' had to be vaccinated
Ham radio network of missionaries reported cases
Key: vaccinated the people around each case (villages with cases, then where it would go next along family and market routes)
Context: 'Four weeks later, there was no more smallpox', months before the mass-vaccination shipment arrived
checks.note: Lasker says 'within 2 weeks'; Grokipedia 'three weeks'. The context follows UW and Emory (four weeks).

checks.claim: Context: share vaccinated given as 7-8 % to under half
Cutter Laboratories, Berkeley, California, licensed 1955 for Salk's killed-virus vaccine
Offit's 2005 account: 'leaving 200 children with varying degrees of paralysis and killing 10'
checks.note: Fitzpatrick's JRSM review of Offit. Other counts differ (Nathanson and Langmuir: 56 paralysed vaccinees plus 113 contacts; CDC over 250 cases), so attributing the figure to Offit is right.

checks.claim: Key: lots passed the required safety tests yet held live virus; the tests were not sensitive enough for small amounts
checks.note: 'despite passing required safety tests'; Grokipedia: tests 'not sensitive enough to catch low viral loads'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: faked tests (no); killed vaccine never safe (IPV the only US polio vaccine since 2000); contaminated after testing (no, inactivation was incomplete)
checks.note: CDC: 'IPV is the only polio vaccine that has been given in the United States since 2000.'

checks.claim: Context: Tripp and Habel found nothing wrong with Cutter's methods; June 1955 hearing blamed 'the lack of scrutiny from the NIH Laboratory of Biologics Control'; NIH director Sebrell rejected Eddy's 1954 report of paralysed monkeys
Context: in 1955 the laboratory became the Division of Biologics Standards; lot-by-lot federal testing
checks.note: NIH timeline: June 1955.

checks.claim: DTP suits rose 'from nine cases between 1978 and 1981 to over 200 by the mid-1980s'
'Only one company was still manufacturing pertussis vaccine in the US by the end of 1985'
Signed 14 November 1986 (Reagan, Public Law 99-660)
Key: makers spared most suits; families paid without proving fault ('a federal no-fault system')
Wrong choices: set fine with no claims; federal grants and free shots; makers pay every claim with juries - none describes the Act
checks.note: Claims go to special masters of the Court of Federal Claims, no jury; paid from a trust fund.

checks.claim: Context: makers stay liable for manufacturing defects and inadequate warnings
checks.note: Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011) barred design-defect suits; warnings carry a presumption of adequacy if FDA rules were met.

checks.claim: Context: 75 cents per dose for each disease prevented (MMR 2.25 dollars); about 5.4 billion dollars paid by 1 September 2025
checks.note: Total from Grokipedia ('As of September 1, 2025'). It is a growing figure, attached to a date, so it survives.

checks.claim: VAERS co-managed by CDC and FDA, established 1990
checks.note: MMWR: replaced the earlier systems on 1 November 1990.

checks.claim: 'Anyone - patients, family members, healthcare providers and vaccine manufacturers - can submit a report'
Context quote: 'A VAERS report alone does not indicate whether a vaccine caused or contributed to an adverse event'
checks.note: Word for word. CDC: VAERS accepts reports 'without judging whether the vaccine caused the adverse event'.

checks.claim: Key: the report shows only that the rash followed the shot; wrong choices (caused it, a doctor checked it, a known side effect) are not shown by one report
checks.note: Strictly, a report records the reporter's account of the timing ('Some reports can lack details or contain errors'); the key is the right simplification.

checks.claim: Context: September 1998 to July 1999, 15 VAERS reports of intussusception after RotaShield; CDC urged suspension 16 July 1999; later studies confirmed the risk
checks.note: Withdrawn October 1999; CDC studies estimated 1-2 extra cases per 10,000 infants.

checks.claim: Early 1980s: seven diseases routinely vaccinated against (diphtheria, measles, mumps, pertussis, polio, rubella, tetanus)
By 2013: 14 pathogens to age 6; up to 24 immunizations by age 2
First half: 'no significant evidence to imply that the recommended immunization schedule is not safe' (stem paraphrase, not in quotation marks)
Key: key elements of the entire schedule 'have not been systematically examined in research studies'
checks.note: The report also says 'few studies have comprehensively assessed' the entire schedule; the key's 'no study had systematically examined' matches the report's own sentence.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: pre-licensure trials, post-licensure monitoring and rare-event studies all existed
Context quotes: 'unethical and infeasible' (an RCT); VSD 'the best available system for studying the safety of the immunization schedule'
HHS (spokesman Andrew Nixon), 1 May 2025: 'All new vaccines will undergo safety testing in placebo-controlled trials prior to licensure'
checks.note: Confirmed via NPR and affiliate copies (search excerpts).

checks.claim: Kennedy quote 'gold standard science' ('every innovation in vaccine development must be grounded in gold standard science and transparency')
Stem: 'Daniel Salmon of Johns Hopkins answered that a new vaccine cannot ethically be compared with no vaccine'
checks.note: Salmon spoke of a new vaccine for a disease that already has one: 'You can't compare that new vaccine to no vaccine, because the standard of care is the old vaccine.' The stem drops that limit and turns it into a rule for every new vaccine. That rule is false: new vaccines for diseases with no vaccine are routinely tested against placebo. Fix: 'Daniel Salmon of Johns Hopkins answered that when a disease already has a vaccine, a new one cannot ethically be compared with no vaccine.'

checks.claim: Steven Black, Prevnar (PCV7) trial in the 1990s; not placebo-controlled because of 'the ethical concern of requiring the more than 15,000 control patients' to get placebo
Key: the controls got a vaccine against a different disease (an investigational meningococcal C conjugate vaccine); 37,868 children, randomised 1:1, double-blind
checks.note: Black et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2000 (abstract via search excerpts).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: older vaccine against the same germ (none licensed for infants), half dose, the new vaccine a year later - not the trial's control
Context: Kennedy told senators he was not proposing to re-test the existing childhood vaccines with placebos
checks.note: His words: 'I'm not suggesting we go back and placebo test all childhood vaccines.' 'Not all' is narrower than 'not the existing ones'. Fix: 'he was not suggesting going back to placebo-test all the childhood vaccines'.

checks.claim: Context: Benn and Kulldorff proposed placebo-controlled trials of approved childhood vaccines ('Proposals for Post-Market Randomized Childhood Vaccine Trials with Ethical Designs', nine trials); Offit called them unethical
checks.note: NOTUS, Margaret Manto, 6 February 2026.

checks.claim: Context: informed consent, the rule since the Nuremberg Code of 1947
checks.note: The Code required the subject's own 'voluntary consent'; parents' consent for a child is the later Helsinki (1964) rule. Acceptable as a simplification, but 'since the Nuremberg Code and the Declaration of Helsinki' would be exact.

checks.claim: Ross Lazarus, Harvard Pilgrim Health Care; AHRQ grant R18 HS017045 (7 Dec 2007 to 29 Sep 2010); a system to detect possible vaccine adverse events in clinic records and report them to VAERS
Final report dated 2010 (Lazarus R., Rockville, MD: AHRQ, 2010)
checks.note: The PDF's file name says 2011.

checks.claim: Key: fewer than 1 in 100 reported. AHRQ summary: 'Adverse events from vaccines are common but underreported, with less than one percent reported to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)'; the report's own text: 'fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported'
checks.note: Stated as background (a reason for the work), not measured by the project, as the context says. The report's own background reads 'Adverse events from drugs and vaccines are common, but underreported'; the context's 'are common but underreported' matches the AHRQ summary word for word.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: 1 in 10, half, nearly all - not what the report said
Context: 35,570 possible reactions, 2.6 % of 1.4 million doses
checks.note: 1.4 million doses of 45 vaccines to 376,452 people, June 2006 to October 2009.

unit_notes: 11 ok, 1 error. Error: a0f30e055e stem gives Daniel Salmon's point as a blanket rule ('a new vaccine cannot ethically be compared with no vaccine'); he spoke of a new vaccine where an older one is the standard of care. Same question: the context's 'not proposing to re-test the existing childhood vaccines' should follow his words 'not ... placebo test all childhood vaccines'. Minor notes: Jesty's sons were later challenged by variolation too (Pead), so the key for 117e29d74b rests on the publication half; Foege's outbreak end is given as 2, 3 or 4 weeks across sources (the context follows UW and Emory); the Nuremberg Code covers the subject's own consent, while parents' proxy consent is Helsinki's.
